questions.stem: Which reaction produces the carbon dioxide that the lungs excrete?

options.explanation: Respiration releases carbon dioxide and water as its wastes.
Building proteins consumes amino acids; it does not release carbon dioxide.
Deamination produces urea, the kidney's cargo, not the lungs'.
Photosynthesis is a plant process and consumes carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Which organ converts surplus amino acids into urea?

options.explanation: Sweat carries traces of urea out, but its source is the liver via the blood.

options.text: In the liver, from excess amino acids
options.explanation: The liver breaks surplus amino acids down, and the nitrogen ends as urea.

options.text: In the kidneys, from filtered blood
options.explanation: The kidneys excrete urea but never manufacture it.

options.text: In the lungs, from carbon dioxide
options.explanation: The lungs handle carbon dioxide and water vapour only.

questions.stem: How does accumulated carbon dioxide damage cells?

options.explanation: Raised pressure is a separate risk-factor story, not the carbon dioxide route.
That is carbon monoxide's trick in the smoking note, not carbon dioxide's here.

options.text: It dissolves to form an acid that lowers pH and slows enzymes
options.explanation: The acidic solution shifts pH and enzymes lose their working range.

options.text: It blocks the nephron filters physically
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide does not clog filters; its harm is chemical.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT excretion?

options.text: Releasing carbon dioxide at the lungs
options.explanation: That is the lungs' excretory role.
Urea is metabolic waste carried out by the kidneys.
Excess ions leaving via sweat fit the excretion definition.

options.text: Passing out undigested food as faeces
options.explanation: Faeces never entered cells, so their removal is egestion.

questions.stem: Why can concentrated body fluids be dangerous to cells?

options.text: They draw water out of cells by osmosis, so reactions falter
options.explanation: The osmotic pull strips cells of the water their chemistry needs.

options.text: They push extra water into cells until they burst
options.explanation: Water flows out of cells into concentrated fluids, not in.
Membranes are not dissolved by concentrated fluids here.

options.text: They cool the cells below enzyme range
options.explanation: The damage is osmotic, not thermal.

questions.modelAnswer: Excretion is the removal from the body of metabolic waste, toxic materials and substances present in excess of requirements.

questions.stem: Name the two wastes of aerobic respiration.
Explain why the build-up of urea would become harmful.
questions.modelAnswer: Urea is a toxic product of the liver's breakdown of surplus amino acids; allowed to accumulate it raises the concentration of the body fluids, drags water out of cells by osmosis and would poison the chemistry that depends on steady conditions.

questions.stem: A student claims breathing out removes 'faeces gases'. Correct the statement using the definition of excretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Breathing out excretes carbon dioxide and water vapour, both genuine metabolic wastes from respiration; faeces are undigested food that never took part in metabolism, so their removal is egestion and belongs to the digestive system, not excretion.

questions.stem: Which organ excretes most of the body's urea?

options.explanation: The liver makes urea but hands it to the blood for the kidneys to remove.
Urea leaves the body dissolved in the urine the kidneys produce.
The lungs send out carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Sweat carries only traces of urea; the main route is urinary.

questions.stem: What leaves the body in sweat?

options.explanation: Carbon dioxide leaves via the lungs, not the sweat glands.
Neither is a sweat ingredient; glucose is reabsorbed in the kidney.

options.text: Water, excess mineral ions and a trace of urea
options.explanation: Sweat is a salty fluid carrying those three things.
Protein is far too large to leave this way.

questions.stem: During exhalation, which excretory products leave the lungs?

options.explanation: Those are inhaled components, not excretory products.
Those travel to the bladder, not the airway.
Water vapour accompanies it and also counts.
Both are wastes of respiration and both leave with used air.

questions.stem: Why does urea travel from the liver to the kidneys rather than being excreted at the liver?

options.text: The liver makes urea and releases it into blood, which the kidneys then filter
options.explanation: Excretion of urea is the kidney's job; the liver only supplies the raw waste.

options.text: The liver has no blood supply
options.explanation: The liver is one of the best-perfused organs in the body.

options.text: Urea becomes harmless in the blood
options.explanation: It stays toxic and must be removed; the kidneys do that.

options.text: The kidneys convert urea back to amino acids
options.explanation: No such conversion happens; urea simply leaves in urine.

questions.stem: Which pairing of organ and cargo is correct?

options.explanation: The liver makes urea; sweating belongs to the skin.
Sweat carries surplus salts out with the water they dissolve in.
The lungs never handle urea.
Carbon dioxide's exit is the airway, not the urinary system.

questions.stem: List the three excretory organs named in the specification.
questions.modelAnswer: The lungs, the kidneys and the skin.

questions.stem: State the excretory cargo of the skin.
questions.modelAnswer: Excess mineral ions, water and small amounts of urea, lost in sweat.

questions.stem: Explain why each excretory organ suits its particular cargo.
questions.modelAnswer: The lungs already handle gas movement, so volatile carbon dioxide and vapour fit naturally; the kidneys filter blood, so dissolved urea and surplus ions are their cargo; the skin's surface glands produce a fluid, so salts and water can simply evaporate away.

questions.stem: After a run, list every excretory route working harder and name what each is removing.
questions.modelAnswer: Breathing deepens and quickens so the lungs expel extra carbon dioxide and water vapour; sweating increases so the skin sheds more water, salts and traces of urea; and the kidneys adjust urine volume, excreting urea and excess ions while conserving water.
